<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To assess whether prenatal exposure to drug treatment for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) increases the risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in children.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population based cohort study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Setting</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nationwide register data on births, dispensed drugs, and specialist healthcare diagnoses from Denmark, Norway, and Sweden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>3 643 376 children born in 2000-21 followed up for a median 9 years after birth in Sweden and 10 years in Norway and Denmark.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Interventions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prenatal exposure, defined as ≥1 filled prescription for ADHD drug treatment anytime during pregnancy or in the second/third trimester (≥98 days after the last menstrual period). Analyses were also done for monotherapy with methylphenidate, amphetamines, and atomoxetine. Unexposed pregnancies had no filled prescriptions for ADHD drugs during pregnancy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Main outcome measures</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neurodevelopmental disorders (any, subgroups, and individual disorders), identified on the basis of inpatient and outpatient diagnoses in specialist healthcare. Propensity score overlap weighted Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate adjusted (weighted) hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Data from Denmark were analysed separately, and results were pooled using random effects meta-analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>7595 (0.2%) children were prenatally exposed to any ADHD drug (5230 methylphenidate, 1510 amphetamines, 553 atomoxetine only). About one third (n=2389) were exposed in the second/third trimester. After control for confounders, neither any nor second/third trimester exposure to ADHD drugs overall or by drug type was associated with increased risk of any neurodevelopmental disorder (weighted hazard ratio 1.05, 95% confidence interval 0.98 to 1.12), behavioural and emotional disorders (1.04, 0.97 to 1.12), or disorders of psychological and intellectual development (1.06, 0.96 to 1.18). Some elevated hazard ratios for infrequent outcomes were observed but not consistently identified across analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This multinational cohort study found no increased risk of childhood neurodevelopmental disorders associated with prenatal exposure to ADHD drugs. These findings strengthen existing evidence and can assist pregnant people and clinicians in weighing the benefits and risks of such treatment during pregnancy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prenatal exposure to drug treatment for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder and risk of neurodevelopmental disorders: Scandinavian multinational cohort study
